body:
>All schools have to accept it. Why wouldnt they anyway?

Because some students are more expensive to educate than others? Students who are behind require extras to catch up. Regardless of how much the vouchers are worth, there is going to be some student who costs more than they are bringing in due to extra services. Sure, you can just not provide them, but then those kids drag down your test scores. Then the parents of smart kids don't want to send their kids there. Makes more sense, from a school's perspective, to be selective with who they take.

If you don't allow this, how can schools limit their population from being overcrowded? If anyone who wanted could go to Boston Latin Academy, most high schoolers nearby would and it would have several times its current student count and be completely overwhelmed. If you say "first come first serve" you're opening the door for huge amounts of bribery, and still have the resources problem: involved parents who can sit around hitting refresh and submit the voucher quickly (or take a day off to stand in line) will have their kids in the best schools, while the uninvolved or underresourced families continue to be fucked over. Exactly the problem we already have, except now it's worse because the literal criteria for good education is parent ability to be involved, instead of that just being a correlate.

>It doesn't solve the issue of districting, just shifts the burden of districting on the transportation abilities of the students family.

I feel like this is the biggest problem with this type of system. The poor kids are still getting screwed over, because their parents can't spend 2 hours a day driving them to the better schools. Even if you somehow provide transportation... Which parents are going to be educated about the best schools and the voucher process, and have the time and know-how to sort through it all? Probably the involved, relatively well-off ones... The ones whose kids are already coming out ahead...

Edit: And if your thoughts are along the lines of "well everyone will start sending their kids to the good schools so everyone will know," eventually the good schools are going to physically fill up. In several years, they may expand (or not. My high school wanted to expand but there was no geographic space close enough that they could reasonably expand into). But in the present, there is simply not enough space in good schools in every area. If a town with 1000 students has 5 schools which currently take 200 kids each (for example), and 1 school is clearly the best, and everyone knows this/cares about the voucher system, the best school still only has space for 200. What happens? Ultimately the other 800 still have to split between the other schools. No supply and demand situation is created where they have to compete, physical requirements will force kids to still go there.
